gloss_terse: Hod — personal name meaning 'splendor' or 'vigor', a descendant of Asher
gloss_readable: A personal name appearing in the genealogy of Asher's descendants. The name derives from the common Hebrew noun meaning 'splendor' or 'vigor,' qualities often celebrated in personal names. Chronicles preserves this individual as part of Asher's tribal lineage, connecting the tribe's identity to divine glory.

senses.1: The multilingual evidence shows this as a proper name with minimal translation variation — English and Spanish transliterate 'Hod' while French and German leave it untranslated in brackets, typical treatment for biblical personal names. Found only in 1 Chronicles 7:37 within Asher's genealogical record.

gloss_terse: Hodevah — variant form of Hodaviah, a Levitical family name
gloss_readable: A Levitical family name appearing in Nehemiah's list of returnees from exile. This represents a variant spelling (Ketiv) of Hodaviah, which appears in the parallel passage in Ezra. Such textual variants between Ezra and Nehemiah are common, as both books draw from similar temple archives but preserve different manuscript traditions.

senses.1: The translations consistently render this as a proper name, with Spanish indicating the family relationship ('of Hodaviah') while English uses the name directly. The prepositional prefix in Hebrew (ל) marks this as 'sons of Hodevah,' indicating a family or clan grouping within the Levitical structure.

gloss_terse: Hoham — Canaanite king of Hebron during Joshua's conquest
gloss_readable: The king of Hebron who joined the southern coalition against Joshua after the fall of Ai and Jericho. As one of five Amorite kings who attacked Gibeon for making peace with Israel, Hoham represents the Canaanite resistance to Israel's entry into the land. His defeat became a key moment in Israel's conquest of the southern hill country.

senses.1: All major translations preserve the name 'Hoham' without variation, reflecting the stability of this proper name in the textual tradition. Joshua 10:3 identifies him specifically as the Hebronite king in the coalition that included Jerusalem, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon.

gloss_terse: madness, folly of an extreme or evil nature
gloss_readable: An intensified form of madness or folly, particularly evil in character. Qoheleth uses this term to describe the progression of a fool's speech — beginning in ordinary folly but escalating to destructive insanity. The word represents an Aramaic-influenced formation, suggesting late composition or foreign linguistic contact in Ecclesiastes.

senses.1: The translations vary: English renders 'madness,' Spanish 'locura' (madness), while French and German leave it untranslated in brackets, perhaps recognizing its textual difficulty. Ecclesiastes 10:13 uses it to describe the culmination of foolish speech, where what begins as mere folly ends in dangerous delusion.

gloss_terse: Homam — son of Seir the Horite, variant of Hemam
gloss_readable: A son of Seir the Horite, representing the pre-Israelite inhabitants of Edom. The name appears in Chronicles' genealogical account with a slightly different spelling than the Genesis parallel, which reads 'Hemam.' Such variant spellings in genealogies reflect different manuscript traditions while referring to the same individual.

senses.1: The translations consistently preserve the proper name with the conjunctive prefix ('and-Homam'), following the Hebrew text's genealogical listing style. The parallel in Genesis 36:22 uses 'Hemam,' with the difference likely representing dialectal variation or scribal updating in Chronicles.

gloss_terse: to consider something easy, make light of
gloss_readable: A rare verb appearing only in Deuteronomy, describing Israel's presumptuous attitude toward invading Canaan despite God's prohibition. The root conveys making something seem easy or trivial, treating a difficult task with inappropriate lightness. Moses recalls how the people 'made light of going up' into the hill country after God had forbidden it.

senses.1: The multilingual glosses show varied attempts to capture this concept: English 'thought easy,' Spanish 'pensasteis que era fácil' (you thought it was easy). The Hiphil conjugation suggests a causative sense — making something appear easy in one's own estimation. Deuteronomy 1:41 uses this to describe Israel's fatal overconfidence.

gloss_terse: Hoshama — abbreviated form meaning 'Yahweh has heard', royal descendant of Judah
gloss_readable: A personal name from Judah's royal lineage, possibly an abbreviated or corrupted form of Jehoshama. The name combines the divine name Yahweh with the verb 'to hear,' expressing thanksgiving that God has heard prayer. Chronicles preserves this descendant among the Davidic line, maintaining the genealogical record of Judah's kings even after the exile.

senses.1: All translations preserve the proper name form without variation. The Septuagint's Greek rendering attempts to capture the Hebrew phonetics. Found only in 1 Chronicles 3:18, this name appears in the post-exilic genealogy of Davidic descendants, suggesting continued hope in the royal line.

gloss_terse: dreaming, raving — used metaphorically of negligent prophets
gloss_readable: A participial form describing those who dream or rave, used metaphorically in Isaiah to condemn Israel's watchmen. The prophet compares false prophets to lazy dogs that lie around dreaming instead of barking to warn of danger. The term suggests both sleep and the delusional speech of someone not fully conscious, emphasizing the prophets' failure to fulfill their duty.

senses.1: Translations consistently render this as 'dreaming' (English, Spanish 'soñando'), though the underlying Semitic root relates to delirious speech. Isaiah 56:10 uses the plural participle to describe prophets who 'cannot bark,' lying down and loving to slumber — dreaming rather than watching for threats to God's people.

gloss_terse: woe, lamentation — textually uncertain term for mourning
gloss_readable: A term for wailing or lamentation appearing in Ezekiel's vision of the scroll. The text itself is quite uncertain — some scholars see it as equivalent to the lament-word 'woe,' while others suggest it relates to the noun for mourning. Ezekiel sees written on both sides of the scroll 'lamentations and mourning and woe,' emphasizing the prophetic burden of judgment.

senses.1: The translation evidence shows significant uncertainty: English 'woe,' Spanish 'ay' (alas), while French and German leave it untranslated. The Septuagint reads 'ouai' (woe). Ezekiel 2:10 lists this as the third term in a triad of mourning vocabulary, all describing the content of God's message of judgment.

gloss_terse: thanksgivings, songs of praise
gloss_readable: Plural form referring to songs or acts of thanksgiving in temple worship. Nehemiah lists this among the liturgical responsibilities of the Levites who led Israel's worship after the return from exile. The term emphasizes the grateful response of a restored community praising God for deliverance.

senses.1: Translations render this as 'thanksgivings' (English) or 'acciones de gracias' (Spanish), capturing the formal liturgical sense. French and German leave it untranslated, perhaps recognizing its technical usage. Nehemiah 12:8 identifies this as part of the Levites' musical ministry, specifically connected to leading congregational praise.

gloss_terse: shining one, morning star — epithet for the king of Babylon
gloss_readable: A poetic epithet meaning 'shining one,' used in Isaiah's taunt against Babylon's fallen king. The phrase 'shining one, son of dawn' employs astral imagery to mock the king's pretensions — once appearing as brilliant as the morning star (Venus), now fallen from heaven. This imagery influenced later interpretations about Satan's fall, though the original context clearly addresses Babylon's historical defeat.

senses.1: Translations vary significantly: English 'shining one,' Spanish 'Lucero' (morning star/Lucifer), reflecting different interpretive traditions. The Assyrian parallel 'muštilil' similarly describes Venus as morning star. Isaiah 14:12 uses this stellar metaphor to portray the dramatic reversal of Babylon's arrogant king, from heavenly heights to Sheol's depths.

gloss_terse: Hemam — son of Seir the Horite, variant of Homam
gloss_readable: A son of Seir the Horite listed in Genesis's genealogy of Edom's pre-Israelite inhabitants. This represents the same individual as Homam in 1 Chronicles 1:39, with the variant spelling reflecting different manuscript traditions. The Horites were the original inhabitants of Seir before Esau's descendants displaced them.

senses.1: All translations preserve the proper name with conjunctive prefix ('and-Hemam'). The parallel in Chronicles reads 'Homam,' with the vowel difference likely representing dialectal variation or textual updating. Genesis 36:22 places this name within Lotan's genealogy, documenting Seir's descendants.

gloss_terse: you wrong, deal harshly with — semantically uncertain verb
gloss_readable: A verb of disputed meaning appearing only in Job's complaint to his friends. The context suggests dealing harshly or wronging someone, though ancient versions and scholars disagree on the precise sense. Job accuses his companions of some repeated offense against him, either causing him wonder through their bizarre accusations or treating him unjustly through their harsh words.

senses.1: Translation evidence shows deep uncertainty: English 'wrong,' Spanish attempts a descriptive phrase about harsh treatment, while French and German preserve the untranslated Hebrew. Some manuscripts read an alternate form. Job 19:3 uses this in Job's protest against his friends' treatment, part of his larger complaint about their failure to comfort him properly.

gloss_terse: expression, look — facial appearance or regard
gloss_readable: A rare noun describing either facial expression or the act of regarding persons. Isaiah uses this term in condemning Judah's brazen sin — even the look on their faces testifies against them, showing no shame. The word's exact sense remains debated: some see it as 'expression' or 'countenance,' others as 'partiality' or 'regarding of persons.'

senses.1: Translations diverge significantly: English 'expression of,' Spanish 'expresión de,' suggesting facial appearance, while ancient versions like Targum and Peshitta understood 'partiality' or 'regarding persons.' Isaiah 3:9 uses this to describe how Judah's public sin is visible even in their faces — they parade their wickedness like Sodom without concealment.

gloss_terse: the one driven far away, removed far off
gloss_readable: A participial form describing someone or something driven far away. Micah uses this in a promise of restoration — God will gather both the lame and those driven far off into a remnant. The image conveys exile and dispersion, with God's people scattered like sheep removed from their pasture, yet destined for regathering.

senses.1: Translations capture the sense of distance and removal: English 'driven far,' Spanish 'alejada' (distanced). Some scholars propose emending the text to 'diseased' or 'exhausted' based on the parallel with 'lame.' Micah 4:7 pairs this with other images of weakness and vulnerability, promising that even the most distant exiles will become part of God's restored kingdom.

gloss_terse: this (feminine demonstrative) — archaic or dialectal form
gloss_readable: An unusual feminine demonstrative pronoun meaning 'this.' Ezekiel uses this archaic or dialectal form when describing how the nations will recognize the restored land of Israel. The form appears to be an emphatic or poetic variant of the standard demonstrative, adding rhetorical weight to the prophet's description.

senses.1: Translations render this as 'this' (feminine): English 'the this,' Spanish 'la esta.' The form is grammatically feminine agreeing with 'land.' Ezekiel 36:35 uses it in God's promise that the nations will marvel at the transformation — 'this land that was desolate has become like the garden of Eden.'

gloss_terse: steps, footsteps — used figuratively for one's life-path
gloss_readable: A plural noun meaning steps or footsteps, used figuratively in Job's description of his former prosperity. The image of steps bathed in cream (or butter) expresses extraordinary abundance and wealth — every step Job took led through rich blessing. This hyperbolic language captures the memory of days when God's favor was manifest in every aspect of his life.

senses.1: All translations preserve the possessive form 'my steps.' The Hebrew uses a first-person suffix on the plural noun. Job 29:6 employs this vivid image alongside other metaphors of abundance — rock pouring out oil, God's lamp shining overhead — to describe the dramatic contrast between his former prosperity and present suffering.

gloss_terse: Helem — personal name of an Asherite, possibly meaning 'strength'
gloss_readable: A personal name from Asher's tribal genealogy. The name may derive from a root meaning 'strength' or 'health,' though its etymology remains uncertain. Chronicles preserves this individual as part of Asher's detailed family records, documenting the tribal structure of northern Israel.

senses.1: All translations preserve the proper name 'Helem' without variation. The name appears without additional identifying information, simply listed among the sons of Heber in Asher's lineage. 1 Chronicles 7:35 places this name within the genealogical framework that establishes Asher's clan structure.

gloss_terse: hammer, workman's mallet
gloss_readable: A hammer or mallet used by craftsmen, appearing in Deborah's song celebrating Jael's victory. The term specifies a workman's tool, not a weapon of war, which makes Jael's act even more striking — she uses common household implements (tent peg and workman's hammer) to defeat Sisera. The detail emphasizes both the improvised nature of her weapon and God's power to deliver through unlikely means.

senses.1: Translations consistently render this as 'hammer' or 'mallet,' with Spanish adding 'martillo de' (hammer of) to capture the construct relationship with 'workmen.' The prepositional prefix 'to/for' marks this as 'to/for the hammer of workmen.' Judges 5:26 uses this in Deborah's poetic celebration of how Jael struck Sisera's temple with an ordinary tool.

gloss_terse: Ham — uncertain place name, possibly ancient Rabbath-Ammon
gloss_readable: A place name of uncertain location where the Zuzim were defeated during the campaign of the eastern kings. The site has not been definitively identified, with suggestions ranging from an otherwise unknown city to an ancient name for Rabbath-Ammon. The text itself shows some uncertainty, as ancient versions offer variant readings.

senses.1: All major translations preserve 'Ham' as a place name with the locative preposition 'in.' The Septuagint and other ancient versions show textual variation, suggesting early uncertainty about this location. Genesis 14:5 lists Ham as one of several battle sites in the trans-Jordanian campaign, providing geographical context for Abraham's later rescue of Lot.

gloss_terse: from their tumult/wealth — textually corrupt or dubious reading
gloss_readable: A highly uncertain term appearing in Ezekiel's oracle of judgment. Scholars debate whether this refers to 'tumult,' 'wealth,' 'moaning,' or represents textual corruption — possibly a scribal duplication of the preceding word. The context describes total destruction where nothing of value remains, but the precise meaning of this term remains elusive.

senses.1: Translation evidence shows radical uncertainty: English 'from their tumult,' Spanish 'de tumulto de ellos,' French 'abondance' (wealth), German leaves it untranslated. The form combines a preposition, a noun, and a pronominal suffix, but many scholars suspect textual error. Ezekiel 7:11 uses this in a litany of loss — 'none of them, none of their multitude, none of their wealth.'

gloss_terse: your raging, turmoil — possibly corrupt text for 'your rebellion'
gloss_readable: A noun meaning turmoil or raging, though the text is widely considered corrupt. The context in Ezekiel suggests God's accusation against Israel for some negative behavior. Many scholars propose emending to 'your rebellion' based on ancient versions and contextual fit, which would make better sense of God's indictment. The reading remains uncertain.

senses.1: Translations attempt various renderings: English 'turmoil of you,' Spanish 'tumulto de ustedes,' French 'bruit' (noise). The Septuagint, Peshitta, and Aquila suggest alternate readings. Ezekiel 5:7 uses this in God's charge against Israel, explaining why judgment must come. Many modern scholars prefer reading 'you rebelled' rather than 'your turmoil.'

gloss_terse: Hamonah — prophetic place name meaning 'multitude', Gog's burial city
gloss_readable: A symbolic place name meaning 'multitude' or 'horde,' designating the city to be founded near Gog's burial site. Ezekiel's vision describes a future battle where God defeats Gog, and the site becomes memorialized by a city named for the multitude buried there. The name itself serves as a monument to God's victory over Israel's enemies.

senses.1: Translations preserve the proper name 'Hamonah,' though its symbolic meaning ('multitude') connects to the context of massive burial. The text itself is considered textually difficult by some scholars. Ezekiel 39:16 uses this name to mark the transformation of a battlefield into a memorial, with the very name testifying to the magnitude of God's judgment on Gog.

gloss_terse: sound, music — specifically of stringed instruments
gloss_readable: A noun denoting sound or music, particularly that produced by stringed instruments like harps. Isaiah uses this in his taunt against Babylon's fallen king, describing how the sound of his harps has descended to Sheol along with his pride. The term emphasizes the cessation of royal celebration and luxury, replaced by the silence of death.

senses.1: Translations render this as 'sound of' (English, Spanish 'sonido de'), indicating the music produced by instruments. The construct form connects directly with 'your harps.' Isaiah 14:11 employs this as part of a mocking lament — everything associated with Babylon's king, including his festive music, has been brought down to the grave beneath him.

gloss_terse: brushwood, kindling — dry twigs for burning
gloss_readable: A plural noun referring to brushwood or dry twigs suitable for kindling fire. Isaiah uses this image in a prayer asking God to manifest His presence with such power that it would be like fire consuming dry brush. The term captures the idea of easily combustible material, emphasizing how quickly and thoroughly God's presence could overwhelm opposition.

senses.1: Translations consistently render this as 'brushwood' (English) or 'ramillas' (Spanish, small branches). The context makes clear this refers to fuel for fire. Isaiah 64:2 (English 64:1) employs this simile asking God to reveal Himself so that nations would tremble, comparing His manifestation to fire setting brushwood ablaze.

gloss_terse: rest, relief — possibly holiday or tax remission
gloss_readable: A noun denoting rest or relief, with uncertain specific application in its sole biblical occurrence. The context in Esther suggests either a holiday celebration, release from taxation, or general amnesty granted by the king for the provinces. The term derives from the verb 'to give rest,' emphasizing a gracious cessation from burden or labor.

senses.1: Translation evidence shows interpretive diversity: English 'relief,' Spanish 'descanso' (rest), with ancient versions suggesting 'release' (Septuagint) or 'rest' (Vulgate). The Septuagint's 'aphesis' could mean release from taxes or debts. Esther 2:18 describes this as part of the king's celebration when he married Esther, extending some form of favor to all the provinces.

gloss_terse: relief, respite — cessation from weeping
gloss_readable: A plural noun meaning relief or respite, specifically from emotional or physical suffering. Jeremiah uses this in Lamentations to describe unceasing weeping — the eye flows continuously without relief or pause. The term emphasizes relentless grief with no opportunity for recovery or rest from sorrow.

senses.1: Translations render this as 'relief' (English) or 'descanso' (Spanish, rest). The root meaning suggests benumbing or cessation. Lamentations 3:49 uses this to intensify the description of mourning over Jerusalem's destruction — tears flow constantly 'without relief, without pause,' emphasizing the depth and persistence of grief.

gloss_terse: perversity, the contrary — reversal of normal order
gloss_readable: A noun meaning perversity, contrariness, or reversal. Isaiah uses this to express shock at Judah's moral inversion — like a potter's clay claiming superiority over the potter. Ezekiel employs it differently, describing Jerusalem's unprecedented reversal of normal prostitution (paying rather than being paid). The term emphasizes things turned upside down from their proper order.

senses.1: Translations in Isaiah render this as 'perversity' with possessive suffix ('your perversity'), expressing outrage at inverted thinking. The word denotes something contrary to natural or moral order. Isaiah 29:16 uses this to condemn the absurdity of creatures questioning their Creator, a fundamental reversal of the Creator-creature relationship.

gloss_terse: overthrow, destruction — specifically of Sodom and Gomorrah
gloss_readable: A noun denoting violent overthrow or destruction, especially associated with the catastrophic judgment of Sodom and Gomorrah. The term became paradigmatic for divine judgment, with later prophets regularly invoking 'the overthrow' as shorthand for total destruction. Genesis uses this to describe God's complete devastation of the cities of the plain.

senses.1: All translations preserve the definite article and render this as 'overthrow' (English) or 'destrucción' (Spanish, destruction). The Assyrian cognate 'abiktu' provides linguistic parallel. Genesis 19:29 uses this to summarize God's judgment on the cities where Lot lived, an event so memorable it became the biblical archetype for divine wrath.

gloss_terse: crooked, perverse — morally twisted path
gloss_readable: An adjective meaning crooked or perverse, describing someone's moral path as twisted and indirect. Proverbs uses this in a saying contrasting the straightforward innocence of the pure with the morally convoluted way of the guilty. The reduplication in the Hebrew form emphasizes the twisted, back-and-forth nature of such a path.

senses.1: Translations render this as 'crooked' (English, Spanish 'tortuoso'), capturing both the literal winding path and the metaphorical moral crookedness. The form uses reduplication for intensification. Proverbs 21:8 contrasts this crooked way of a guilty person with the straight path of the pure, using spatial metaphor to describe moral character.

gloss_terse: deliverance, rescue — particularly from danger or oppression
gloss_readable: A noun meaning deliverance or rescue, appearing in Esther's pivotal moment when Mordecai warns that silence may cost her life. The term carries the hope that rescue will come from somewhere, even if not from expected sources. This reflects the book's theme of hidden providence — God's name never appears, yet deliverance arrives.

senses.1: All translations preserve the conjunctive prefix and render this as 'deliverance' (English) or 'liberación' (Spanish). The form may show Aramaic influence, fitting Esther's Persian court setting. Esther 4:14 uses this in Mordecai's famous statement that deliverance for the Jews will arise 'from another place' if Esther remains silent, hinting at divine providence without naming God directly.

gloss_terse: weapons, arms — meaning uncertain, possibly textual corruption
gloss_readable: A noun of highly uncertain meaning, possibly referring to weapons or military equipment, though the text may be corrupt. Context in Ezekiel suggests military invasion, and ancient versions offer varying interpretations including 'weapons,' 'from the north,' or 'with rattling.' Modern scholarship remains divided on whether to emend the text or accept one of the proposed meanings.

senses.1: Translation evidence shows radical divergence: English 'weapons,' Spanish 'armas' (weapons), French 'arme,' yet the Septuagint suggests 'from the north' while Peshitta and Targum read 'with arms.' Ezekiel 23:24 describes invading forces, but this term's precise contribution remains unclear. The Assyrian connection proposed by some scholars is debated.

gloss_terse: Hara — uncertain place name, possibly variant for 'cities of the Medes'
gloss_readable: A place name of uncertain location listed among the destinations of exiled Israelites. The site appears only in Chronicles with no parallel in Kings, leading scholars to suspect textual corruption. The most common proposal emends this to 'cities of the Medes,' matching the parallel passages in 2 Kings that describe Assyrian deportation locations.

senses.1: Translations preserve 'Hara' as a place name with conjunctive prefix ('and-Hara'), but scholarly commentary widely questions this reading. The parallel passages in 2 Kings 17:6 and 18:11 omit this name, instead reading 'cities of the Medes.' 1 Chronicles 5:26 lists this among the Assyrian deportation sites for the Transjordanian tribes.

gloss_terse: altar-hearth, the upper part of the altar where fire burns
gloss_readable: The altar-hearth or upper platform of the altar where the sacrificial fire burned. Ezekiel's vision of the restored temple includes precise measurements of this component. The term may derive from combining 'hearth' with 'El' (God), meaning 'hearth of God.' This represents the most sacred part of the altar where offerings were consumed by holy fire.

senses.1: Translations vary in handling this technical term: English 'altar-hearth,' Spanish 'hogar' (hearth), French 'autel' (altar). The text shows variation between Ketiv and Qere readings. Ezekiel 43:15 uses this in detailed specifications for the altar's construction, with the hearth forming the top level where sacrifices were burned before God.

gloss_terse: pregnant women — used in war atrocity description
gloss_readable: An adjectival noun referring to pregnant women, appearing in prophetic judgment oracles describing war atrocities. The term emphasizes the complete brutality of military conquest, where even the most vulnerable — expectant mothers — face violence. This became a standard element in ancient Near Eastern descriptions of total warfare.

senses.1: Translations consistently render this as 'pregnant women' with possessive suffix: English 'their pregnant women,' Spanish 'sus embarazadas.' The Assyrian cognate 'êriiâtê' provides linguistic parallel. Hosea 13:16 uses this in describing Samaria's coming judgment, where military invasion will bring complete devastation including the horrific targeting of expectant mothers.

gloss_terse: fancies, imaginings — thoughts or visions in dreams
gloss_readable: An Aramaic noun meaning fancies or imaginings, specifically the mental images experienced in dreams. Daniel uses this term to describe Nebuchadnezzar's troubling nocturnal visions that prompted his summons of the wise men. The word emphasizes the vivid, image-laden quality of dream content that demands interpretation.

senses.1: Translations render this as 'thoughts' (English, Spanish 'pensamientos') or 'dreams' (French 'rêve'). The Aramaic plural form appears in the context of disturbing visions. Daniel 4:5 uses this to describe the mental images that troubled the king's sleep, prompting his desperate search for someone who could explain their meaning.

gloss_terse: the Harorite — probably textual error for 'the Harodite'
gloss_readable: A gentillic adjective designating someone from an otherwise unknown location Haror. The text is almost certainly corrupt, as the parallel passage in 2 Samuel reads 'Harodite' (from Harod). Chronicles apparently preserves a scribal error where the 'd' was misread or miscopied as 'r.' The reference identifies one of David's mighty warriors by hometown.

senses.1: All translations preserve 'Harorite' with the definite article, but scholarly consensus favors emending to 'Harodite' based on the 2 Samuel 23:25 parallel. No place called Haror is known elsewhere. 1 Chronicles 11:27 lists this as the hometown designation of Shammoth, one of David's elite fighting men, the Thirty.

gloss_terse: ruins — concrete remains of destruction
gloss_readable: A plural noun denoting ruins in the concrete sense — the physical remains of demolished buildings. Amos uses this in God's promise to restore the fallen booth of David, raising up not just the structure itself but also its ruins. The term pairs with 'breaches,' together emphasizing complete restoration from total devastation.

senses.1: Translations consistently render this as 'ruins' with possessive suffix: English 'its ruins,' Spanish 'sus ruinas.' The parallel term 'breaches' reinforces the image of comprehensive destruction. Amos 9:11 employs this in the famous promise to 'raise up the booth of David that is fallen,' including restoration of all its ruined parts — language later applied to messianic hope.

gloss_terse: your ruin, your destroyed land
gloss_readable: A noun denoting overthrow, destruction, or ruin, used in construct form with 'land.' Isaiah employs this in God's promise to restore Zion, referring to 'the land of your ruin' — the homeland that had been devastated. The term emphasizes the land's state of destruction from which God promises to bring renewal and repopulation.

senses.1: Translations render this as 'destruction' (English, Spanish 'destrucción') with second-person feminine suffix ('your'). The parallel terms 'your waste places' and 'your desolations' reinforce the theme of devastation. Isaiah 49:19 uses this in promising that even Zion's ruined land will become too small for its returning inhabitants, transforming disaster into overcrowding from blessing.

gloss_terse: Horam — Canaanite king of Gezer who aided Lachish
gloss_readable: The king of Gezer who came to aid Lachish during Joshua's conquest of southern Canaan. Unlike the five kings who formed the anti-Gibeonite coalition, Horam appears later in the narrative, attempting to relieve Lachish when Joshua besieged it. His intervention proved futile, as Joshua defeated both him and his army, extending Israel's control over the southern hill country.

senses.1: All major translations preserve the proper name 'Horam' consistently across languages. Joshua 10:33 records his arrival to help Lachish and his subsequent defeat, though notably Gezer itself was not captured at this time — the city remained unconquered until much later in Israel's history, showing Joshua's campaign had limits even in victory.
